# About the Author {.unnumbered}

**Dave Rosenman** is a software engineer and data scientist with a Bachelor of Science in Physics from The College of New Jersey. He builds production analytics software, much of it in R: Shiny applications used daily by the people who depend on them, data pipelines, and the packages that make both easier to write. He is the author of orbitr, the package this book is built on, and of other open-source packages on CRAN and PyPI, among them `sqlserverconnect`, a set of helpers for connecting R to SQL Server, and `dbexplorer`, a Shiny application for browsing and exporting database tables.

Before moving into industry he worked as a scientist for the State of New Jersey, at the Department of Environmental Protection, where he co-authored the *2016 New Jersey Integrated Water Quality Assessment Report*, the state's Clean Water Act assessment of the condition of its rivers, lakes, and coastal waters, submitted to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. The job was equal parts science and software: turning years of monitoring data into defensible assessments, with code that had to be right because decisions were made on it. That combination, physics training applied through well-engineered software, is the approach this book takes.

He is currently an Infrastructure and Operations Engineer at Optum, and is working toward a Master of Science in Computer Science at Georgia Tech, specializing in artificial intelligence.

<!-- DAVE: add the PyPI package name(s) if you want them listed alongside the
     CRAN ones. -->

*Orbital Mechanics with R* grew out of the orbitr documentation and the questions it could not answer: not how to run an orbit, but why the simulation behaves the way it does. He also writes about physics for a general audience. He lives in Newtown, Pennsylvania.

## Where to find things {.unnumbered}

- **orbitr documentation:** <https://orbit-r.com> — the package reference, the articles, and the interactive app. Start here for how any function works.
- **GitHub:** <https://github.com/DRosenman> — the package source (`orbitr`), this book's source (`orbitr-book`), and his other open-source work. Bug reports and pull requests for either go there.
- **Personal site:** <https://daverosenman.com> — projects, writing, and contact.

If you use the book in a course, or build something with the package, he would like to hear about it.
